questions.question: For the linear vector ODE $\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)$ with constant $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$, suppose $A\boldsymbol{v}=\lambda\boldsymbol{v}$ with $\boldsymbol{v}\neq\boldsymbol{0}$. Which function is then a solution?
For $\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)$ with constant real $A$, which condition on the eigenvalues of $A$ is equivalent to the origin being asymptotically stable?
options: Every eigenvalue has negative real part
At least one eigenvalue has negative real part
Every eigenvalue has real part at most $0$

questions.question: In $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ with real $A$, an eigenvalue $\lambda=\alpha+i\beta$ with $\alpha,\beta$ real and $\beta\neq0$ contributes the factor $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}$ to the solutions. What do $\alpha$ and $\beta$ control?
options: $\alpha$ sets growth or decay via $\mathrm{e}^{\alpha t}$; $\beta$ sets the angular speed
$\beta$ sets growth or decay via $\mathrm{e}^{\beta t}$; $\alpha$ sets the angular speed
Solutions scale like $\mathrm{e}^{|\lambda|t}$, so even $\alpha<0$ modes grow
Size is governed by $|\lambda|^{t}$, so modes decay exactly when $|\lambda|<1$

questions.question: Which statement about equilibria of $\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)$, with $A$ a constant $n\times n$ matrix, is correct?
options: $\boldsymbol{0}$ is one only if all eigenvalues have negative real part
Every eigenvector of $A$ is an equilibrium
$\boldsymbol{0}$ is one only if $A$ is invertible
$\boldsymbol{0}$ is always one; it is the only one if $A$ is invertible

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{v}_1,\dots,\boldsymbol{v}_n$ be an eigenbasis of $A$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$. The solution of $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$, $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is $\sum_i c_i\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_it}\boldsymbol{v}_i$. How are the $c_i$ found?
options: Take $c_i$ to be the $i$-th component of $\boldsymbol{x}_0$

questions.question: Solve $\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(1,3)^{\top}$. Which $\boldsymbol{x}(t)$ is the solution?
Classify the equilibrium $\boldsymbol{0}$ of $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ for $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\2&-1\end{pmatrix}$, whose eigenvalues are the complex pair $-1\pm2i$.
options: Asymptotically stable: solutions spiral in to $\boldsymbol{0}$
Stable but not asymptotically stable, since solutions rotate
Not decidable from the eigenvalues, since they are not real

questions.question: A two-dimensional system $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ has $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ with one positive and one negative eigenvalue, $4$ and $-2$. What is the stability of the origin?
options: Asymptotically stable, as the eigenvalue $-2$ is negative
Unstable, as the eigenvalue $4$ has positive real part
Stable but not asymptotically, as the eigenvalues have opposite signs

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, which function solves $\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)$?

Both eigenvalues of $A=\begin{pmatrix}\tfrac{1}{2}&3\\0&-\tfrac{1}{4}\end{pmatrix}$, namely $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $-\tfrac{1}{4}$, lie inside $(-1,1)$. Is the origin of the continuous-time system $\boldsymbol{x}'(t)=A\boldsymbol{x}(t)$ stable?
options: Asymptotically stable, because the trace $\tfrac{1}{4}$ is below $1$

questions.question: For the system $x_1'=-x_1+x_2$, $x_2'=-2x_2$ with $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(1,1)^{\top}$, a student writes $x_1(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ from the first equation. Why is this wrong?
options: The first rate must be $-2$, the largest coefficient in absolute value
It is correct; each row can be solved on its own
$x_1'$ also depends on $x_2(t)$, which is not identically $0$
All components must share one rate, here $\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$ from $x_2$

questions.question: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$, the only eigenvalue is $2$ and every eigenvector is a multiple of $(1,0)^{\top}$. Which statement about the solutions of $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ is correct?
options: Some solutions contain a term $t\mathrm{e}^{2t}$, e.g. $(t\mathrm{e}^{2t},\mathrm{e}^{2t})^{\top}$
Every solution is $c\mathrm{e}^{2t}(1,0)^{\top}$, as $2$ is the only eigenvalue
No solution exists unless $\boldsymbol{x}_0$ is a multiple of $(1,0)^{\top}$

options: $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\mathrm{e}^{\bar\lambda t}\bar{\boldsymbol{v}}$, real because $A$ is

questions.question: $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&2\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvectors $(1,0)^{\top}$ for $-1$ and $(1,-1)^{\top}$ for $-3$. Which function solves $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ with $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(2,1)^{\top}$?

For $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\1&-2\end{pmatrix}$ (invertible) and constant $\boldsymbol{b}=(3,0)^{\top}$, what is the equilibrium $\boldsymbol{x}^*$?
Writing $x''+3x'+2x=0$ as $\boldsymbol{y}'=A\boldsymbol{y}$ with $\boldsymbol{y}=(y_1,y_2)^{\top}=(x,x')^{\top}$, which matrix is $A$?
For $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$, suppose every eigenvalue of $A$ has real part $\le0$ and some has real part exactly $0$. What else is needed for the origin to be stable?
options: Nothing more; real parts $\le0$ already imply that the origin is stable
All eigenvalues of $A$ must be distinct, so that none repeats
$A$ must be invertible, so that $0$ is not an eigenvalue
Zero-real-part eigenvalues need equal algebraic and geometric multiplicity

questions.question: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1\pm i$. Which function solves $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ with $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(1,0)^{\top}$?

For $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{b}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&-2\end{pmatrix}$, $\boldsymbol{b}=(1,4)^{\top}$, equilibrium $\boldsymbol{x}^*=(3,2)^{\top}$, and eigenvectors $(1,0)^{\top}$ for $-1$, $(1,-1)^{\top}$ for $-2$: which solution has $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(3,0)^{\top}$?
For $\boldsymbol{x}'=A\boldsymbol{x}$ with $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, the solution with $\boldsymbol{x}(0)=(0,1)^{\top}$ tends to $\boldsymbol{0}$. What follows about the origin?
options: It is asymptotically stable, as a solution converges to it
It is stable but not asymptotically stable
$(0,1)^{\top}$ must be an equilibrium, since its solution converges
It is unstable: other solutions, e.g. from $(1,0)^{\top}$, grow.
